intro.afterNote: Below: the moment, then what CoachOS runs instead — under your name, after you approve.

categories.title: Website & presence
categories.sub: when the only proof you exist is a feed

items.title: No real website, so a prospect can't verify you're legitimate
items.quote: Someone asked for my website on a Tuesday and I sent them my Instagram. She said thanks, that's great, and then just — nothing. It's the ones that don't come through that you never hear about.
items.after: Tuesday's "what's your website?" gets a real link — fast, specific, with booking built in

items.title: A missed domain renewal takes the whole business offline
items.quote: The email went first. Then a client rang to say my site was showing a page of adverts. The renewal notices had been going to an address on that same domain — and the card on file had expired in January.
items.after: Renewal notices come to us, and the card on file is ours to watch. The site simply stays up

items.title: The handle available on one platform is already gone on the next
items.quote: I'm one thing on Instagram, the same thing with an underscore on TikTok, and something completely different on LinkedIn. A client messaged an account using my old logo and got nothing back.
items.after: One name, every platform, old accounts cleaned up — your printed cards match the internet again

categories.title: Marketing & visibility
categories.sub: what happens when client work gets busy

items.title: Posting stops the moment client work picks up — and nobody notices until the pipeline does
items.quote: I checked the analytics on a Tuesday and realised the last thing I'd posted was in March. It's May. I signed two clients in April and just stopped. Enquiries kept trickling in off older stuff for a while. They've stopped now.
items.after: Three weeks into a full cohort, the feed is still publishing — you approved it two Sundays ago, in ten minutes

items.title: Feast-or-famine repeats because marketing only restarts once the pipeline is already empty
items.quote: January and February I was turning work away. By April I was down to two clients, so I started posting again. That work landed in June — by which point I was flat out and stopped doing all of it. Fourth year running.
items.after: The June work lands while April is still busy — because the posting never stopped

items.title: Generic positioning gets lost in an increasingly crowded field
items.quote: Someone at a networking thing asked what I do and I said 'executive coaching, mainly leadership and confidence' — and watched her face do absolutely nothing. The other two coaches in the room said more or less the same.
items.after: The networking answer takes one sentence now. Faces react. Referrals follow

categories.title: Leads & follow-up
categories.sub: what happens to an inbound lead in the wild

items.title: A callback within two hours can still lose to one within twenty minutes
items.quote: The enquiry came in at 9:40 and I rang back at half eleven. Two hours — felt fine to me. She was lovely about it. Said she'd already booked a call with someone for Thursday.
items.after: The 9:40 inquiry gets a 9:44 reply — booked before the coffee's done

items.title: The average business takes 42 hours to respond to its own leads
items.quote: The contact form goes to an inbox that also gets invoices, newsletters, and whatever the accountant is sending. Found four quote requests sitting in there once, the oldest from Monday.
items.after: Quote requests stop sharing a room with invoices. The oldest unanswered lead is minutes old, not from Monday

items.title: Most small businesses track leads on a spreadsheet, or nowhere at all
items.quote: Somebody messaged in November asking about corporate sessions and I replied from the train. Meant to log it that evening. Found the thread again in February — she had followed up once and I never saw it.
items.after: Every conversation reads booked, declined, or waiting — and nothing waits long

categories.title: Sales & closing
categories.sub: what kills a deal that felt basically done

items.title: Deals that closed needed far more follow-up than most people ever attempt
items.quote: I sent two emails and decided she wasn't interested. Found out in March she'd signed with someone else — someone who emailed her six times. I sat there looking at my sent folder.
items.after: Touches three, five, and seven go out on schedule, warm and specific. Polite no longer means gone

items.title: A booked call is not the same as a call that happens
items.quote: The two o'clock on Thursday is the one that gets me. I clear the hour before it, read the intake form, sit there with the link open. Then nothing — and at twelve past I send the message I keep saved, because I send it so often.
items.after: The Thursday two o'clock shows up — reminded yesterday, confirmed this morning

categories.title: Programs & structure
categories.sub: mentoring without a system underneath it

items.title: Years of mentoring, and still no real answer when someone asks what you offer
items.quote: A woman at my nephew's christening asked what I do, and eleven years in, I heard myself say 'it depends.' I can tell you exactly what happened with any one of my mentees. I can't tell you what the thing is that I sell.
items.after: The christening question gets a one-line answer with a price in it — and a page to send afterward

items.title: Manual matching tops out at 25–50 people — most cohorts are bigger
items.quote: Cohort one was 32 people and I did the matching in an evening. Cohort two was 58 and took a whole weekend — and on Sunday night I found I'd matched someone with her own line manager. Cohort three is meant to be 90.
items.after: Cohort three's ninety people: matched in days, zero line managers paired, zero Sunday redos

items.title: A satisfaction score is not a number a CFO can act on
items.quote: The finance review is in November and the only real number I have is 4.2 out of 5, from a survey most people ignored. The CFO asked what would happen if we didn't run the program.
items.after: November's finance review gets participation, goals met, and outcomes per pair — sitting next to the budget line they defend

items.title: Marketplace fees quietly take a much bigger bite than the headline rate
items.quote: I only worked it out because I was doing my tax return and the numbers didn't match what I thought I'd earned. Gross was fine. Then the commission, then the Connects, then the wire fee every month.
items.after: The tax return matches what you actually earned. Nothing is skimmed between the work and the money

items.title: Paying for a lead does not mean being the only one who paid for it
items.quote: The notification came in at 7:40. I paid for the lead, wrote a proper reply inside four minutes. She already had three others, one at half my price. I never heard back from her at all.
items.after: The 7:40 lead is yours alone — nobody else paid for her, and the reply was out by 7:44

items.title: A paid community can still leave every real question unanswered
items.quote: Seventy-nine a month. I've asked four questions since March — two got a thumbs-up emoji, and one got answered by somebody warming me up to sell me something. I ended up back on Google anyway.
items.after: Questions get answers from people running real practices — because nobody else got in

arcs.title: The whole arc
arcs.intro: Single problems get single fixes. Most people arrive with five tangled together — here's how a full engagement runs, and what's different at the end.

items.title: The coach with a full roster and an empty pipeline
items.arrives: A calendar full for this cohort and silent for the next one. Feed dead since week three, inquiries landing on a page that still says "coaching services," follow-ups living in her head.
items.weeks: Strategy call and the one-sentence positioning first. Then the site rebuilt around her specialty, handles unified, a content calendar drafted from her own thinking, and lead management switched on — every inquiry answered in minutes, even mid-session.
chips: Marketing no longer stops when coaching starts
The next cohort fills while this one runs

items.title: The freelancer in year four of feast-or-famine
items.arrives: The same annual shape every year — busy spring, empty April, panic posting, June recovery. Two-email follow-ups, marketplace commissions eating the margin.
items.weeks: Rate and niche strategy, then a portfolio site off the marketplaces. Referral asks timed to happy clients, content publishing while he delivers, the eight-touch follow-through running on every open deal, one pipeline view.
chips: The pipeline fills during delivery months, not after them
Deals stop dying at touch two
Nothing skimmed between the work and the money

items.title: The HR lead with a 90-person cohort and a spreadsheet
items.arrives: Matching that eats a weekend and still pairs someone with her line manager, no visibility into which pairs meet, and a 4.2-out-of-5 to show the CFO.
items.weeks: Criteria workshop, the whole cohort matched in days with conflicts caught before pairing, light session tracking with quiet-pair flags in week six, and a per-pair outcomes report ready for the finance review.
chips: Problems fixed in week 6, not found at the survey
A number the budget can stand on
